title:
Comment of Lancee Whetman in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 11/2/2026

documents.name: 152140.txt
documents.text:
Lancee Whetman, Anchorage, AK.
November 2, 2026

Debbie-Anne A. Reese
Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street NE, Room 1A
Washington, DC 20426

Re: DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC; Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted for Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions To Intervene, and Competing Applications

Dear Secretary Reese,

On behalf of the Alaska Marine Community Coalition (AMCC), thank you for the opportunity to comment on the preliminary permit application filed by DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC (DeepGreen). AMCC is a fishermen-founded organization working to advance sustainable fisheries, healthy marine ecosystems, and thriving fishing communities across Alaska. A subset of our members fish or reside in Upper Cook Inlet and on the Kenai Peninsula.

AMCC respectfully asks that FERC deny the application because the Project could harm (A) the endangered Cook Inlet beluga whale; (B) salmon migration; (C) commercial fishing access; and (D) safe marine travel.

BACKGROUND

On February 11, 2026, DeepGreen applied for a preliminary permit to study the feasibility of a project in the Upper Cook Inlet, East Foreland Corridor, Kenai Peninsula Borough. Project electricity would power a subsea data center; only “spare” electricity, if any, “could” go to the grid. The Project would include approximately 330-350 marine hydrokinetic turbines; 66 modular subsea-compute pods; a 3.5-mile, 115 kV hybrid power/fiber-optic subsea cable; and a cable landing in the Nikiski Industrial Corridor, between the Agrium Kenai Nitrogen Operations and the Kenai Liquefied Natural Gas Plant.

A preliminary permit would only preserve DeepGreen’s application priority and allow feasibility study. But AMCC opposes the Project because it could harm beluga critical habitat, water temperatures, and prey species, and could disrupt safe passage for fishermen, marine mammals, and fish in Cook Inlet’s narrow East Foreland Corridor.

THE PROJECT COULD HARM BELUGAS, SALMON, FISHING ACCESS, AND SAFE MARINE TRAVEL

The Endangered Cook Inlet Beluga Whale

The Cook Inlet beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas) is genetically distinct and resides in the Inlet year-round. Listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) since 2008, it has not recovered. The population is estimated at 331 whales and remains threatened by pollution, habitat degradation, harassment, and interactions with human activity. The ESA requires designation of critical habitat, meaning areas “essential to the conservation of the species,” and defines “conservation” as the use of all methods and procedures necessary to bring a listed species to the point where ESA protections are no longer necessary. 

The Project would lie within Critical Habitat Area 2. As Exhibit 2 shows, its roughly three-mile footprint would sit in Nikiski’s East Foreland Corridor, Cook Inlet’s narrowest point. Under 50 C.F.R. § 226.220, essential features of this habitat include (1) coastal waters near anadromous fish streams; (2) adequate prey, including Pacific salmon (Chinook, sockeye, chum, and coho), eulachon, Pacific cod, walleye pollock, saffron cod, and yellowfin sole; (3) protection from harmful toxins; (4) unrestricted movement between critical habitat areas; and (5) sufficiently low underwater noise to prevent whales from abandoning these areas. Any project in critical habitat must be carefully evaluated to ensure it does not destroy or adversely modify it.

The Project could affect every one of these features. First, it could raise water temperatures. Data centers generate enormous waste heat; on land, they can raise air temperatures by 16°F nearby and up to 4°F in adjacent neighborhoods. Fish are ectothermic, so their metabolism and activity depend on surrounding water temperature. Warmer water also holds less dissolved oxygen and increases the solubility of metals and other toxins. DeepGreen proposes a 48-month baseline study for belugas, but that would not predict thermal effects on the prey they depend on.

Second, data centers can contribute to pollution, including per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), or “forever chemicals,” which do not readily break down in the environment or the body. Long-term exposure is linked to cancer, hormone disruption, and developmental and reproductive problems. PFAS bioaccumulate and biomagnify up the food chain, posing severe risks to belugas and the ecosystem.

If FERC nonetheless grants a permit, DeepGreen should be required to conduct site-specific studies for belugas, all five Pacific salmon species, and other commercially harvested species, examining whether turbines, moorings, cables, and construction alter fish behavior, interfere with migration, affect sensitive habitats, or create cumulative effects over the Project’s life.

Salmon Migration

The East Foreland Corridor is a natural bottleneck through which adult salmon bound for the Kenai, Kasilof, Susitna, and other rivers, and juveniles moving seaward, must pass, especially near the eastside set net (ESSN) fishery. The Project would place hundreds of turbines, dozens of subsea pods, moorings, and a 115 kV cable in this corridor. These structures could injure fish, alter flow and sediment transport, and redirect migrating salmon. Electromagnetic fields may disrupt migratory fishes’ orientation, and continuous noise and vibration could cause avoidance, delay upstream movement, and increase stress and energy expenditure.

A delayed, diverted, or diminished run would affect the ESSN fishery, other commercial harvesters, subsistence and personal-use fishermen, and sport anglers, and could compound harm to belugas that rely on salmon. If FERC grants a permit, it should require study of migration timing, route use, behavioral responses, and mortality risk for all five salmon species across multiple seasons and run years, in consultation with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, the National Marine Fisheries Service, and affected fishing communities.

Commercial Fishing Access

Commercial, sport, and Alaska Native subsistence fishermen rely on Cook Inlet for all five salmon species, as well as razor clams, Pacific herring, and smelt. In Upper Cook Inlet alone, more than 1,300 limited-entry permits have been issued for drift and set gillnet fishing, about 10% of all salmon permits statewide. It is one of the most active fisheries in the state, supporting livelihoods, local businesses, food security, and cultural traditions.

The turbine array, associated infrastructure, and cable landing could restrict access to traditional fishing areas, interfere with gear deployment and retrieval, and create navigational hazards where fishermen already operate with little margin. AMCC members fish adjacent to the proposed landing site, and a landing zone there could create new conflict between industrial infrastructure and fishing gear, vessel access, and operations. FERC should consider whether the Project would compound existing constraints on fishermen operating near established industrial facilities. Any loss of grounds or access could harm permit holders, crew, processors, and other dependent businesses.

Safe Marine Navigation and Vessel Traffic

Cook Inlet is known for powerful tidal currents. Kenai Peninsula Borough Mayor Peter Micciche has described “screaming eight-knot” currents and questioned the project’s viability. These conditions warrant an independent assessment of engineering feasibility, navigational safety, and effects on fishing vessels, including current speeds and variability, tidal cycles, sediment movement, vessel maneuverability, emergency access, and the ability of fishermen to safely navigate around Project infrastructure.

The Inlet also carries heavy traffic, including cargo vessels, tankers, passenger vessels, tugs, fishing vessels, and government, survey, and research vessels. Most movement occurs along the east side. Fishing vessels are the most numerous, while tugs spend the most operational time in the Inlet. The Forelands, where the Project is proposed, is one of the Inlet’s primary passage lines. The Project could significantly disrupt these corridors, affecting fishermen and others who depend on safe, predictable access.

CONCLUSION

DeepGreen’s application raises the same concerns voiced in Maine, where the Eastport city manager called a similar DeepGreen proposal “the equivalent of an idea scrawled on a bar napkin.” Opponents there warn that thermal pollution could make the bay unlivable for lobsters, damage fishing and tourism, and harm North Atlantic right whales, fin whales, and other wildlife. Maine groups also warned that preliminary surveys could increase vessel traffic and underwater noise, disrupting whale communication and feeding.

Although a preliminary permit does not authorize construction, it preserves DeepGreen’s priority for a proposal with substantial potential consequences for beluga critical habitat and Cook Inlet’s fisheries. A 48-month baseline study alone cannot ensure the Project’s long-term effects on temperature, noise, marine mammals, fish, and fishing access will be understood or mitigated. AMCC respectfully urges FERC to deny the application. Protecting Cook Inlet requires a precautionary approach that prioritizes ecological integrity, safe marine passage, and the long-term health of Alaska’s fisheries and communities.

Thank you for considering AMCC’s comments.

Sincerely,

Michelle Stratton, Executive Director
Lancee Whetman, Fisheries Program Manager
